Faithless describes someone — or something — that has broken faith. "Breaking faith" means violating the trust, loyalty, or commitment that was expected of them. The word points directly at a betrayal of something that was owed.

Faithless has two closely connected meanings:

The first and most common meaning is: disloyal; not keeping one's promises or commitments. This is the sense you will encounter most often in everyday life. A faithless person was entrusted with loyalty — through a relationship, a duty, a promise, or a role — and chose to betray it. The betrayal can be toward a person, a group, a cause, or a responsibility.

A faithless partner is someone in a romantic relationship who cheats on or betrays their partner. A faithless ally is a friend or partner who abandons you when you count on them the most. A faithless leader is someone in a position of authority who betrays the people they were supposed to serve. Notice the pattern: in every case, someone was given trust, and they broke it.

The second meaning is: without religious faith; not believing in God or religion. This sense is more formal and literary, and you'll find it more often in religious texts, older writing, or poetry than in everyday conversation. "He preached to a faithless generation" means he preached to people who had lost or abandoned their religious belief. This usage carries less of a moral sting than the first — it's closer to a plain description of an absence of belief, though in religious contexts it can still carry disappointment or sadness.

Both meanings share the same root idea: the absence of faith — whether that's faith in a person (loyalty), or faith in God (belief).

"Faithless" is not a neutral word. It carries serious moral weight, especially in its first meaning. When you call someone faithless, you are not simply saying they were forgetful, unreliable, or inconsistent. You are saying they broke a deep, meaningful bond — one they knew they were bound to honour. There is a strong sense of deliberate betrayal in the word. The person knew what loyalty or commitment was expected of them, and they turned away from it anyway.

This makes "faithless" a harsh, heavy word. It is not something you'd say lightly.

The adjective can describe a person ("a faithless friend"), a group or generation ("a faithless people"), an act or quality ("faithless behaviour"), or even abstract things like promises made without any real intention of being kept ("faithless vows"). It can also occasionally describe a thing or institution that has failed in its duty.

There is also a specific legal and political term worth knowing: a faithless elector. In the United States Electoral College system, an elector is a person chosen to cast a formal vote for president. A "faithless elector" is one who votes for a different candidate than the one they pledged to support — they broke their commitment. This is a real, documented usage of the word.

It helps to place "faithless" on a scale:

Unreliable → Disloyal → Faithless → Treacherous

Someone unreliable simply can't be counted on — they might forget, be inconsistent, or fail to follow through, but not necessarily out of any ill intent. Someone disloyal didn't stand by you — they may have put their own interests first or stopped supporting you. Someone faithless violated a genuine, serious bond — a vow, a duty, a heartfelt commitment. They betrayed your trust in a meaningful way. Someone treacherous goes even further — they actively worked to harm you through their betrayal, often with calculation and deception.

"Faithless" sits in the upper range of this scale. It is a serious accusation.

Unfaithful is the closest synonym and is nearly interchangeable, but it is more commonly used in romantic contexts — an unfaithful spouse, for example. "Faithless" has a broader, slightly more formal reach and can apply to duties, causes, and beliefs beyond just romance.

Disloyal is similar but somewhat softer. Not everyone who is disloyal has made an explicit, solemn commitment, whereas "faithless" implies that the bond was real and known.

Treacherous is stronger and implies active harm — not just abandoning someone, but working against them.

Perfidious is the most formal and literary equivalent; it means deceitful and habitually untrustworthy, often over a long period of time.

False (as in "a false friend") is a milder, more general term for someone who pretends loyalty while not actually offering it.

The natural opposite of faithless is faithful — loyal, keeping one's promises, and steadfast in commitment. Other opposites include loyal (unwavering in allegiance), trustworthy (reliably keeping commitments), devoted (deeply and sincerely committed), and true (in its literary sense of reliable and honest, as in "a true friend").

To really absorb a word, seeing it used in different contexts is essential:

"She discovered that her faithless friends had shared her secrets the moment she left the room."

"The faithless soldier deserted his post in the middle of the battle, leaving his comrades behind."

"History remembers faithless rulers not for their power, but for their betrayals."

"The old preacher lamented that he lived in a faithless age, when people had turned away from belief."

"He proved faithless to every promise he ever made — his words simply didn't mean anything."

"A faithless ally is worse than no ally at all, because they give you a false sense of security."

If you want to carry just one idea away: faithless means having broken a bond of trust, loyalty, or commitment — or, in its religious sense, having no belief in God. It is a word that judges. It does not merely describe someone who failed; it names them as someone who betrayed something real and meaningful. Use it carefully, because it carries weight.
